PRELIMINARY DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment relationship problem
Preliminary determination
[1] This preliminary determination determines the applicant’s, Selectlok New Zealand
Limited’s (Selectlok’s), application for an interim injunction against the first respondent, Mr
Colin Pearce, and the second respondent Keyless Solutions Limited (Keyless).

2
Interim injunction sought by Selectlok
[2] Selectlok sought (among other things) that the respondents be restrained from operating
Keyless until Selectlok’s substantive claims have been resolved or determined by the
Authority. Selectlok set out in its submissions the terms of the requested interim injunction as
follows:
(a) That [Mr Pearce] cease trading […] Keyless and abide by the terms of his
employment agreement;
(b) Undertakings from Mr Pearce that he, nor any other person, will not operate [Keyless]
during the proceedings;
(c) Undertakings that the [Respondents] will retain all records from the date of
incorporation of [Keyless].
The respondents’ position
[3] The respondents opposed the interim injunction application and said no grounds exist
to support an interim injunction. The respondents also said there was no legal basis for the
Authority to issue the undertakings Selectlok had sought. They also denied Selectlok’s
substantive claims and associated remedies.
[4] Mr Pearce denied all of the claims Selectlok made against him. In particular, Mr Pearce
denied breaching his duty of fidelity and/or duty of good faith to Selectlok while he was
employed by it. Mr Pearce denied breaching his post-employment confidentiality obligations
and/or non-solicitation post-employment restraint that applies until 30 September 2026.
[5] Mr Pearce pointed out that he was not bound by a post-employment non-competition
or non-dealing restraint.
[6] Keyless denied Mr Pearce had breached his employment agreement, and it denied
aiding and/or abetting him to do so. The respondents also denied that Keyless operated in
competition with Selectlok.
The parties
[7] Selectlok started in 2002 initially as a division of Seletrix Australia. Mr Michael
Saunders, one of Selectlok’s two directors, purchased Selectlok in 2014 with his then wife, at

3
which time it became a New Zealand owned company. Selectlok’s other director is Wendy
Dunsmore. Selectlok’s shares are held by a family trust.
[8] Selectlok provides locking, hinging and sealing solutions suited to New Zealand
applications and conditions. It also supplies products such as gas struts, handles, locks, latches,
hinges and sealing rubber among other things. Selectlok sources products from its sole agencies
and strategic supplier partnerships worldwide and it supplies customers nationwide and
internationally.
[9] Mr Pearce started work for Selectlok in 2002. From 13 October 2003 until he retired
on 31 March 2026 Mr Pearce was Sales Area Manager. The Authority was provided with a
copy of his employment agreement which was dated 1 July 2012. His role required him to
source hardware or items that Selectlok’s customers requested from its overseas suppliers.
[10] Keyless was incorporated on 10 March 2023. Mr Pearce is the sole director and
shareholder in Keyless, but he said Keyless is his son’s business. Colin Pearce said Keyless
was only registered in his name because his son, Jonathan Pearce and wife Erin Thompson,
were at that time in the process of applying for a mortgage. Their mortgage broker had said
Jonathan being a director and shareholder of Keyless would have meant they could not have
obtained finance for a property purchase. Colin Pearce therefore said he helped his son out by
registering Keyless under his (Colin’s) name.
[11] Colin Pearce did not inform Selectlok about this, and he said he did not consider
Keyless or himself (due to his limited involvement) to be in competition with Selectlok. Colin
Pearce described his involvement in the operations of Keyless to be “extremely limited, if not
non-existent”.
[12] Mr Pearce described his involvement with Keyless being limited to being a director and
shareholder ‘on paper”, and to “occasionally sending/receiving emails. He said he is not
“actively involved in running the company”. He also said that now he was retired he would
“occasionally assist Jonathan (but not in a way that would conflict with [his] post-employment
restraints.”
[13] Mr Pearce denied Keyless was in competition with Selectlok as they operated in
“materially different markets”, so “did not compete in the same market for the same customer
demand.”

Mr Pearce’s employment agreement
[18] Mr Pearce’s employment agreement dated 1 July 2012 contained the following material
clauses:
(a) Clause 5 Employee Fidelity
(b) Clause 18 Confidential Information
(c) Clause 26 Intellectual Property
(d) Clause 34 Non-Solicitation.
[19] Mr Pearce’s employment agreement did not contain a post-employment non-
competition and/or non-dealing clause.
[20] Clause 5 stated:
5.1 The Employee agrees to place his/her duties to the Employer above all other
business activities. The Employee shall not carry out work of the type being carried
out for the Employer for others. If in the reasonable opinion of the Employer there
exists a conflict or other reasonable grounds for abandoning or curtailing outside
activities, the Employee shall abandon or curtail such activities if so directed.
5.2 The Employee may engage in other activities such as University studies,
personal business, charitable or professional work provided such external activities
or interests do not interfere with the Employee’s performance of their duties or
obligations to the Employer or compete with its business (as may be determined
solely by the Employer) and the Employee shall inform it forthwith of any such
potential conflicting or competing external activities or interests.
[21] Clause 18 stated:
18.1 The Employee undertakes not to, at any time or for any reason, use or
disclose to any person any confidential information he or she may obtain regarding
the Employer’s business including any trade secrets and client information and other
commercially sensitive or valuable information, except with the express permission
of the Employer.

6
18.2 The Employee undertakes not to remove, copy or destroy any confidential
records or data of the Employer, without the permission of the Employer.
18.3 The Employee undertakes not to disclose to any person, or make use of, any
information or material regarding the details of any client or employee of the
Employer that has been obtained during the course of his/her employment.
18.4 The Employee shall not disclose any confidential information to any other
employee who is not authorised to receive it.
18.5 The Employee shall not use or disclose, or attempt to use or disclose, any
confidential information relating to the Employer’s business for their own benefit, as
distinct from the benefit of the Employer, or in any manner which may injure or cause
loss whether directly or indirectly to the Employer.
18.6 The restrictions contained in the preceding clauses under this heading do not
apply to:
(a) The use or disclosure of such information as may be reasonably
necessary to enable the Employee to fulfil their obligations for the Employer;
or
(b) Information which has already become public knowledge other than
as a result of a breach of this clause by the Employee.
18.7 The restrictions contained in the preceding clauses under this heading apply
both during the term of this Agreement and after the termination of the employment.
18.8 On cessation of employment the Employee shall forthwith return all
property, documents, records, software, data, or programmes of the Employer
(including copies of the same) and shall not retain any such property.
[22] Clause 26 stated:
26.1 Any original work and other material produced or to be published by the
Employee and arising from the employment with the Employer shall remain the
property of the Employer, which shall have full rights to such work, process, design

7
or other material whether those rights are exercised in any form or not during the
employment or on cessation of the employment.
[23] Mr Pearce’s non-solicitation clause applied for six months after his employment ended,
so it expires on 30 September 2026.
[24] Clause 34 of Mr Pearce’s employment agreement stated:
34.1 The Employee shall not at any time during the period of employment or for
a period of six months after termination of employment, for whatever reason, either
on the Employee’s own account or for any other person, firm, organisation or
company with which the Employee associated, directly or indirectly, in any capacity
whatever:
(a) Solicit, endeavour to entice away from, or discourage from being
employed by the Employer, any other employee or actual
supplier/client/customer or prospective supplier/client/customer of
the Employer or in any way or by any means interfere or seek to
interfere with the relationship between the Employer and its
suppliers/clients/customers and employees, for any service supplied
or to be supplied by the Employer; or
(b) Seek business referrals from any person, firm or company that has
referred business to the Employer during the term of the Employee’s
employment.
The Authority’s investigation
[25] Selectlok’s ex-parte application was declined but the interim injunction application was
granted urgency. The parties attended mediation, but that did not resolve this matter.
[26] This interim injunction application has been determined ‘on the papers’. Selectlok
lodged two affidavits from Mr Saunders; affidavits from current employees Amond Findlay
and Euta Mose; and an affidavit from a former employee, Arash Bahadori.
[27] On 29 July 2026 Selectlok lodged a memorandum regarding subvention payments.
[28] Mr Pearce lodged two affidavits, the second of which included taxation information.
The respondents also lodged a memorandum on taxation issues on 30 July 2026.

8
[29] Both parties lodged written submissions.
Selectlok’s evidence
[30] In May 2026 Selectlok discovered documents on Mr Pearce’s former work computer
that indicated his involvement with Keyless. That led Selectlok to arrange for an IT search of
Mr Pearce’s former work computer which discovered Keyless’ bank statements from May
2023 to March 2025.
[31] Selectlok say Keyless’ bank statement showed it had received approximately
$111,047.27 from two of Selectlok’s customers (referred to in this determination as LSC and
WLS). Selectlok also saw approximately $60,630.14 from other potential Selectlok clients that
Keyless had placed orders for. There were also deposits totalling $32,623.48 into Keyless’ bank
accounts from LockLab Limited (LockLab), of which Jonathan Pearce is the sole director and
shareholder.
[32] Keyless’ bank statements from March 2025 to date were missing from Selectlok’s work
computer. However, Mr Pearce provided them as part of the evidence lodged in this interim
injunction application.
[33] Selectlok relies on this information to claim that Mr Pearce has diverted more than
$200,000.00 of sales from Selectlok to Keyless.
[34] Amond Findlay was employed by Selectlok as a Sales Representative in 2011 and after
Mr Pearce’s retirement in March 2026, Mr Findlay subsequently became the Sales Manager.
Mr Findlay said that a key part of the Sales Manager’s role included:
(a) Providing support to Selectlok’s customers;
(b) Expanding Selectlok’s customer base;
(c) Expanding the type of products that Selectlok supplies.
[35] Euta Mose has been employed by Selectlok since July 2022, initially as a Storeman but
in December 2025 he was promoted to Warehouse Manager. Mr Mose said Mr Pearce asked
him to package consignments of locks or associated products to send to a business [KNK]
which did not have Selectlok on the paperwork.

9
[36] Mr Mose reported that he had referred queries from existing clients asking for “a certain
type of lock that did not include a physical key” to Mr Pearce, who reportedly said there was
no market for these types of locks. Mr Mose did not identify when this had occurred, what type
of lock was involved, or whether Keyless sold the requested lock.
[37] A former employee, Arash Bahadori was employed by Selectlok from September 2019
to December 2025, initially as a Storeman but then soon after that as Warehouse Manager. Mr
Bahadori said he had observed Mr Pearce on unspecified date(s) bring parcels to Selectlok’s
premises which according to the paperwork were not sales by Selectlok or deliveries to it. He
also reported seeing Mr Pearce filling the rubbish bin at the premises with empty courier and
delivery boxes which had Keyless on them.
The respondents’ evidence
[38] Mr Pearce lodged two affidavits; the first affidavit was for himself and the second
affidavit was lodged by him on behalf of Keyless, as its sole director and shareholder.
[39] Mr Pearce’s second affidavit produced tax documentation, which included the tax
returns from March 2023 to March 2026 the respondents had lodged with IRD and for Pearce
Group Holdings Limited (Pearce Group).
[40] Mr Pearce is the sole director and shareholder of Pearce Group, which is an investment
company that owns the factory building rented out to LockLab (which owned and operated by
Jonathan Pearce) for its workshop, and also to Keyless for storage purposes. Pearce Group has
made losses since its incorporation and no taxable income has been earned for distribution to
shareholders since 1 March 2023.
[41] Keyless lodged a $0.00 tax return with Inland Revenue for the period from its
incorporation on 10 March 2023 to 31 March 2023. For the Financial Year Ended (FYE) 31
March 2024, Keyless made a loss of $21,114.85 which was carried forward into the 2025 tax
year. This loss from FYE was carried forward to offset Keyless’ taxable income for FYE 2025,
which was then transferred to Pearce Group as a subvention payment. No income was
distributed to Mr Pearce from Keyless as at 31 March 2025.
[42] For the FYE 31 March 2026, Keyless had a taxable profit which was transferred to
Pearce Group as a subvention payment. No income was distributed to Mr Pearce at 31 March

10
2026. No shareholder salaries were paid to Mr Pearce from

Relevant law
[46] The Authority’s power to grant interim injunctive
established legal test requires consideration of three
questions:
(a) Is there a serious question to be tried.
(b) Where does the balance of convenience lie.
(c) Where does the overall justice of the case lie.
[47] Restraint of trade provisions are prima facie
unenforceable
as reasonably necessary to protect proprietary interests of the
interest.1

11
[48] The onus lies on the party asserting the reasonableness of the restraint and the restraint
must be no wider than is reasonably necessary to protect the legitimate interest.2
[49] Selectlok therefore bears the onus of establishing on the balance of probabilities that it
has a legitimate proprietary interest which is capable of being protected after Mr Pearce retired,
or which is subject to an enforceable post-employment restraint.
Issues
[50] The following issues are to be determined at this interim stage of these proceedings:
(a) Does Selectlok have an arguable case that:
(i) Mr Pearce has breached his employment agreement?
(ii) Keyless has aided and abetted Mr Pearce to breach his employment
agreement?
(b) If so, where does the balance of convenience lie pending the resolution of
Selectlok’s substantive claims?
(c) What does the overall justice of the situation require from now until the
substantive claims are resolved/determined?
(d) What if any interim orders should be made?
(e) What costs should be awarded?
Does Selectlok have an arguable case?
Legitimate proprietary interest?
[51] Selectlok had a legitimate proprietary interest in:
(a) Protecting the relationships it had with its employees, clients, customers and
suppliers for a limited period after Mr Pearce retired.
(b) Preventing Mr Pearce from disclosing and/or using its confidential information
after his employment had ended
2 Transpacific Industries Group (NZ) Ltd v Harris [2013] NZEmpC 97 at [41] and [44].

12
Reasonableness of the post-employment restraints
[52] The six months’ non-solicitation restraint period was reasonable for someone in Mr
Pearce’s senior role and the indefinite restraint on him disclosing and/or using Selectlok’s
confidential information (in the nature of trade secrets and commercially sensitive or valuable
information) was also reasonable given the nature of his role.
[53] Accordingly, clauses 18 and 34.1 of Mr Pearce’s employment agreement were
reasonable and therefore enforceable.
Arguable breach of “Employee Fidelity” clause in the employment agreement?
[54] Selectlok has an arguable case that Mr Pearce breached:
(a) Clause 5.1 of his employment agreement while employed by “carrying out work
of the type being carried out [by Selectlok] for others.” And
(b) Clause 5.2 of his employment agreement by not “informing [Selectlok]
forthwith of any potential conflicting or competing external activities or
interests.”
[55] Although the respondents denied Keyless and Selectlok were in competition because
they operated in distinct market segments, Selectlok did not accept that. Clause 5.1 is drafted
broadly to cover the “type” of work, namely the supply of locks.
[56] The Authority was therefore satisfied on a plain wording interpretation of clause 5 that
it appeared likely that Selectlok and Keyless were carrying out the same “type” of work,
because they were both in the business of providing locks and associated products to customers
in New Zealand.
[57] It was therefore arguable that Mr Pearce breached clause 5.2 of his employment
agreement by not informing Selectlok, before he reserved Keyless’ name with the Companies
Registrar on 1 March 2023, that he was going to be the sole director and shareholder of his
son’s business that involved the provision of locks to residential clients in New Zealand.
[58] Clause 5.2 of Mr Pearce’s employment agreement gave Selectlok the power to
exclusively determine whether an employee was competing its business. By failing to disclose
his association and (what he said was limited) involvement with Keyless, Mr Pearce effectively

13
deprived Selectlok of the ability to properly assess his view that Keyless was not competing
with Selectlok before Keyless was incorporated.
[59] Because Mr Pearce was not subject to a non-compete or non-dealing post-employment
restraint his duty of fidelity ended when his employment ended on 31 March 2026.
[60] The dispute between the parties about whether Selectlok and Keyless were in
competition or operated in different markets will need to be resolved after a substantive
investigation meeting has been held. The available evidence established Selectlok’s customers
are commercial and industrial businesses requiring hardware for vehicle bodies, toolboxes,
trailers and electrical switchboards.
[61] The Authority noted that Mr Pearce’s job description with Selectlok was detailed, but
it did not include expanding the range of products Selectlok supplied. Selectlok’s own
catalogue and its website confirm its product range is mechanical hardware components for
commercial and industrial applications. Subject to the observation below, that product range
does not include smart locks.
[62] “I loq” is a smart lock (without a physical key). The “I loq” product did not appear in
Selectlok’s catalogue of products offered or on its website. Selectlok’s evidence that it did sell
smart locks (meaning keyless locks) was weak as it relied on assertions that Mr Pearce’s
evidence had fundamentally undermined. For example, Selectlok’s claim it sold I loq’s was not
supported by any evidence it had made even one sale of an “I loq” product to any customer in
New Zealand.
[63] The I loq Mr Saunders claimed was sold by Selectlok and Keyless was not the same or
substantially similar to the smart lock Keyless sold. Selectlok’s lock was designed for
commercial and industrial applications (such as server racks and telecommunications cabinets)
compared to the residential smart locks Keyless sold. Keyless sold smart locks and custom-
made accessories designed to suit the smart locks for installation in New Zealand residential
homes. These products Keyless sold were not available to the general/public market and are
not products Selectlok supplies.
[64] Mr Pearce’s specific and detailed evidence that Selectlok and Keyless sold different
products, in different markets, to different customers was preferred over the limited, vague and
non-specific assertions Selectlok made. The currently available evidence only suggests that

14
Selectlok and Keyless both operate within the same type of industry, namely the broader lock
or access-related sector.
[65] An employee cannot be restrained from engaging in a business that provides different
goods or services in a different market simply because both business may fall within the same
broad industry category.
[66] It would have been up to Selectlok’s directors to change the company’s policy to
provide products and services to residential and property managers (as clients/customers). That
would have involved strategic decisions about the direction of the company that was outside
the scope of Mr Pearce’s role. Setting the strategic direction of Selectlok was not part of his
job description.
Arguable breach of confidential information clause in the employment agreement?
[67] The confidential information obligations in clause 18 of Mr Pearce’s employment
agreement apply indefinitely, so they continued after his employed had ended on 31 March
2026.
[68] Clause 18.1 prevented the use or disclosure of confidential information including trade
secrets and client information and other commercially sensitive or valuable information
without Selectlok’s express permission.
[69] In Faccendia Chicken Ltd v Fowler & Ors the English Court of Appeal identified three
categories of information an employee could have obtained as a result of their employment.
These three categories of employment related information have been adopted by New Zealand
courts:3
(a) Information which is easily accessible from public sources, which is not
confidential and which the employee may use at any time.
(b) Information which the employee has been told is confidential, or which is so
obviously confidential because of its nature or character, but which is also
information which remains in the employee’s head and is part of their own skill
and knowledge which they use in the course of their employment.
3 Faccendia Chicken Ltd v Fowler [1985] 1 All ER 724 (CA).

15
This information cannot be disclosed by an employee while employed, but they
may use all of their own skills and knowledge for their own benefit after the
employment relationship has ended. This sort of information may be able to be
protected by an express restraint which is stated to continue after the termination
of an employee’s employment.
(c) Trade secrets which are so confidential they cannot be used by the employee to
benefit anyone but the employer.
[70] The Employment Court in Trans Pacific Industries (NZ) Ltd v Harris and Smart
Environmental Ltd held information that is clearly intended to remain confidential, but which
is not necessarily as strictly confidential as trade secrets may still be protected.4
[71] It was up to Selectlok to explain what information it considered fell within the
confidentiality clause in Mr Pearce’s employment agreement, why it believed he had disclosed
or misused Selectlok’s confidential information, and how and when that had occurred. A mere
assertion that confidential information exists and has been disclosed/misused by Mr Pearce is
insufficient to establish clause 18 of his employment agreement has likely been breached.
[72] Mr Saunders’ two affidavits did not address what if any confidential information Mr
Pearce was alleged to have disclosed and/or misused.
[73] Mr Pearce in his first affidavit denied breaching his post-employment confidentiality
obligations, so although Mr Saunders was aware of that, he still failed to identify what specific
confidential information Selectlok alleged Mr Pearce had disclosed or misused.
[74] The affidavits produced by Selectlok’s other witnesses, in addition to Mr Saunders’
affidavits, also failed to provide specific evidence establishing what confidential information
Mr Pearce had allegedly disclosed/used; which clients/customers/suppliers he had allegedly
solicited; or how and when this had occurred in breach of clauses 18 and or 34.1 of his
employment agreement.
[75] Even if the evidence the other Selectlok witnesses gave in their affidavits was correct,
that simply established Mr Pearce may have sent couriers and/or disposed of cardboard boxes
that did not have Selectlok’s information on them. These affidavits from other Selectlok
4 Trans Pacific Industries (NZ) Ltd v Harris & Anor [2013] NZEmpC 97 at [38].

16
witnesses were heavy on the inferences but failed to provide any actual evidence that Mr Pearce
had breached his post-employment non-solicitation and confidentiality obligations.
[76] If Selectlok was able to establish that Mr Pearce had disclosed or misused its
confidential information then it could apply for a compliance order, provided there was
evidence of an actual breach having already occurred, as opposed to speculation that a breach
could have potentially occurred or may in future occur.
[77] An application for an interim injunction to prevent a third party such as Keyless (that
has no contractual obligations to Selectlok) from operating or continuing to trade is anti-
competitive. Compelling evidence of wrongdoing by Keyless that needed to be restrained in
order to prevent ongoing harm to Selectlok was required but has not been provided by Selectlok
in its five affidavits.
[78] Nor did Selectlok identify what intellectual property Mr Pearce had which it alleged he
had disclosed and/or misused. The mere assertion by Selectlok that while employed Mr Pearce
had access to (unspecified and not particularised) intellectual property does not support its
claim that a breach of post-employment restraints has occurred or that an interim injunction
needed to be issued.
[79] To be arguable, a claim must have an evidential foundation. Selectlok’s failure to
provide specific evidence that Mr Pearce had breached the confidential information clause in
his employment agreement, meant that claim cannot be said (at least at this time) to be arguable.
Arguable case non-solicitation clause was breached?
[80] Clause 34.1(a) of Mr Pearce’s employment agreement imposed a six months’ post-
employment restraint on soliciting or enticing away any employee, actual
supplier/client/customer or prospective supplier/client/customer or otherwise interfering with
Selectlok’s relationship with its suppliers/clients/customers and employees for any service
supplied or to be supplied by Selectlok.
[81] Clause 34.1(b) for six months post-employment prevented Mr Pearce from seeking
business referrals from any person, firm or company that has referred business to Selectlok
while he was employed.

17
[82] The non-solicitation clause does not prohibit contact with or proximity to Selectlok’s
customers, because it is limited to solicitation. The non-solicitation restraint in clause 34.1 of
Mr Pearce’s employment agreement cannot be ‘stretched’ to cover potential or theoretical
competition.5
[83] The reference to a “prospective” supplier/client/customer is to be read as applying to
those who Selectlok was in the process of making a supplier or client/customer while Mr Pearce
was employed. It does not relate to any supplier or any person/entity that may any time in the
future purchase a lock. The legitimate proprietary interest that the non-solicitation clause
covers has to have an actual connection with Selectlok and for it to be reasonable it must also
relate to Mr Pearce’s employment.
[84] For example, if Mr Pearce was involved in helping Selectlok obtain a prospective new
supplier (but no supply contract had been entered into by the time his employment ended), or
if he had been helping to obtain a new client/customer, then that particular “prospective”
relationship could reasonably be protected by Selectlok for a limited time. However, the non-
solicitation clause would be unreasonable, and therefore void on public policy grounds, if it
attempted to prevent Mr Pearce from soliciting suppliers, clients/customers that had previously
had no connection with Selectlok.
[85] Mr Pearce’s first affidavit put Selectlok on notice he had not breached the non-
solicitation obligations in clause 34.1 of his employment agreement. Despite being on notice
of that, Mr Saunders in his two affidavits failed to identify what solicitation Mr Pearce had
allegedly engaged in, or how and when that had occurred.
[86] Selectlok also failed to identify when Mr Pearce had allegedly interfered with the
relationship(s) Selectlok had with its clients/customers/suppliers or which person, firm or
company Mr Pearce had allegedly solicited business for Keyless from. That was a fundamental
omission, because an interim injunction must be based on credible evidence, not merely
assumptions or speculation.
[87] Mr Pearce said that after 1 April 2026 he had one telephone conversation with a
Selectlok client (BS) solely because BS had been a friend and colleague for 20 years. There
5 Skids Programme Management Ltd v McNeill [2012] NZCA at [65] (CA).

18
was no evidence or even allegation by Selectlok that one phone call by Mr Pearce had involved
solicitation of BS.
[88] Keyless did not engage in any active marketing, as it operated by way of a passive
website only, or clients were referred by Jonathan’s contacts and/or previous dealings with
him.
[89] Mr Pearce said Keyless did not have any customers who could directly or indirectly be
customers of Selectlok, because Keyless offers digital access control products (such as smart
lock and smart cylinders) which are not products or services Selectlok offered, at least while
Mr Pearce was employed by it. It was significant that Selectlok did not provide any evidence
it was now selling these products, or intended to do so in the immediate future.
[90] Keyless also supplied its products to end users (such as residential customers and
property managers, and sometimes locksmiths who installed the locks). Selectlok supplied
hardware products, including locks, latches, hinges, seals and gas struts and handles to mainly
commercial customers and industrial businesses that need hardware for manufacturing,
fabrication, transport, cabinetry, and similar uses. These therefore appeared to involve different
markets, different product offerings, different services and a different client base. Evidence of
an overlap in these areas was absent.
[91] The supplier Mr Saunders identified in his first affidavit had not previously been used
by Selectlok so that allegation cannot support a claim clause 34.1 (a) had been breached by Mr
Pearce.
[92] After reviewing the available evidence, the Authority concluded Selectlok has failed to
provide evidence to support its claim that Mr Pearce had breached his non-solicitation post-
employment obligations. The absence of any such evidence meant Selectlok was unable to
establish there was an arguable case that Mr Pearce had done so.
Is there an arguable case against Keyless?
[93] The arguable case criteria is a low bar to clear. Selectlok’s claim that Keyless aided and
abetted Mr Pearce to breach the Employee Fidelity clause in his employment agreement cannot
be said to be frivolous or vexatious. However, that obligation did not survive the end of Mr
Pearce’s employment on 31 March 2026.

19
[94] Selectlok faced the same problems regarding its claims that Keyless had aided and
abetted Mr Pearce to breach his two post-employment restraints (that related to non-solicitation
and confidential information) that it did with these claims against Mr Pearce. Namely, Selectlok
failed to provide evidence to establish it was more likely than not that these alleged breaches
had occurred, were occurring or were likely to occur and that Keyless had aided and abetted
Mr Pearce’s breaches of his employment agreement.
[95] Accordingly, Selectlok was unable to establish that it had an arguable case that Keyless
had aided and abetted Mr Pearce’s breaches of his post-employment restraints.
Outcome of the arguable case criteria
[96] There is an arguable case Mr Pearce breached his duty of fidelity to Selectlok and/or
clause 5 of his employment agreement while he was still employed. However, those obligations
ceased when Mr Pearce’s employment ended on 31 March 2026.
[97] Selectlok was required to produce evidence of the alleged breaches by Mr Pearce of his
post-employment restraints, as opposed to merely asserting such breaches had occurred, which
is what it has done. In the absence of such evidence, Selectlok was unable to establish it had
an arguable case that post-employment restraints had been breached by Mr Pearce and that
Keyless had aided and abetted those alleged breaches.
[98] Accordingly, Selectlok has failed to establish on the balance of probabilities it had an
arguable case that Mr Pearce had breached clauses 18 and/or 34.1 of his employment agreement
or that Keyless had been involved in that.
Where does the balance of convenience lie?
Evidence of post-employment breaches
[99] Selectlok failed to establish that the non-solicitation restraint and the ongoing
confidentiality obligations in Mr Pearce’s employment agreement, along with his undertaking
to comply with them, were insufficient to adequately protect its legitimate proprietary interests.
[100] Selectlok also failed to identify to the Authority any particular or specific confidential
information (in the nature of trade secrets and/or commercially sensitive and valuable

20
information) that Mr Pearce continued to carry in his head as a result of his employment which
could inadvertently be disclosed by him, so needed to be restrained.
Mr Pearce’s circumstances
[101] Mr Pearce is retired. He has not earned any income since he retired. Mr Pearce had a
minimal ‘on paper’ role with Keyless, which is his son’s business. He denied breaching his
post-employment restraints and there was no evidence provided by Selectlok to establish that
he likely did so.
[102] Mr Pearce has undertaken to comply with clauses 18 and 34.1 of his employment which
contain the post-employment restraints, so that undertaking weighs against the need for an
interim injunction to be issued.
Lack of IT evidence
[103] Selectlok has undertaken an IT search of the computer Mr Pearce used while employed
and no evidence of him removing Selectlok’s information or confidential information was
discovered. The employment relationship appeared to have ended on good terms and there was
no evidence of any ill will between the parties that could potentially motivate Mr Pearce to
harm Selectlok.
Adequacy of current post-employment restraints
[104] Based on the currently available evidence, the post-employment restraints that are
currently in place appear sufficient to protect Selectlok’s legitimate proprietary interests. Mr
Pearce understood his obligations to Selectlok and advised he was willing to comply with them.
[105] Even if Mr Pearce had commercially sensitive confidential information (noting
Selectlok had not identified or specified exactly what that was) there was no evidence to
establish that any such information remained current to date. Because the employment ended
four months ago any information Mr Pearce had retained in his head would likely not still be
up to date. Therefore the risk of an inadvertent breach by Mr Pearce appeared low to nil.
Inadequacy of Selectlok’s evidence
[106] Although Selectlok believed Mr Pearce has breached his post-employment restraints,
its failure to provide evidence of that meant Selectlok’s claims (at least as at this stage in the

21
Authority’s investigation) are speculative and appear based on feelings or assumptions rather
than demonstratable breaches of Mr Pearce’s post-employment obligations.
[107] Selectlok may subsequently be able to produce evidence to a substantive investigation
meeting to support its claims that breaches of post-employment restraints have actually
occurred at, but for now the Authority is limited to assessing this interim injunction application
based on the evidence the parties have actually provided to date. In Selectlok’s case, its
evidence has fallen short of what was required in order to support an interim injunction being
issued.
Different products sold
[108] With the exception of lithium batteries, Selectlok failed to identify one product or item
in Keyless’ catalogue that it also sold. In terms of the sale of lithium batteries by both
companies, the evidence established these were more likely than not fundamentally different
products.
[109] Selectlok sells lithium batteries used in jump packs, which are designed for high-power
automotive, commercial, and industrial applications, whereas the lithium batteries Keyless
sells are used in smart locks designed for low power security and access control applications.
Accordingly, the currently available evidence suggests the lithium battery products Selectlok
and Keyless sell are different products that serve materially different purposes and customer
markets.
Anti-competition
[110] After reviewing the currently available evidence, the Authority was left with the
impression that Selectlok’s interim injunction application is anti-competitive in circumstances
where it elected not to impose a post-employment non-competition or non-dealing restraint on
Mr Pearce to prevent him, for a period of time after his employment ended, from competing
with it.
Adequacy of damages
[111] Damages would likely be an adequate remedy if Selectlok establishes at a substantive
investigation meeting that Mr Pearce has breached his contractual obligations. However,
currently there is insufficient evidence to establish on the balance of probabilities that:

22
(a) Selectlok sells any product or service that Keyless also currently sells.
(b) Selectlok intends in the immediate future to sell any of the products (or services)
that Keyless currently sells.
(c) Any client/customer/supplier has actually been solicited by Mr Pearce for his,
and/or Keyless’, benefit.
(d) Mr Pearce had likely actually interfered with the relationships Selectlok has with
its current or prospective employee/clients/customers/suppliers.
(e) Mr Pearce having disclosed or misused any of Selectlok’s confidential
information.
Duration of the enforceable restraints
[112] The confidentiality obligations are indefinite but the non-solicitation restraint expires
on 30 September 2026. The substantive investigation meeting will not be held before October
or November 2026, so it would not be appropriate to issue an interim injunction for the period
Selectlok has claimed.
Adequacy of undertakings
[113] Mr Pearce’s undertaking and post-employment restraints appear sufficient to protect
Selectlok’s legitimate proprietary interest until its substantive claims are resolved or
determined.
Outcome of the balance of convenience criteria
[114] The balance of convenience factors favour the status quo being maintained, so that
weighs against an interim injunction being issued.
What is the overall justice of the situation?
[115] At this point the Authority has to stand back and assess where the overall justice lies
pending resolution or determination of Selectlok’s substantive claims. That involved an
objective balancing of the rights, obligations and inconveniences involved for all of the parties
and for third parties who could be adversely affected if an interim injunction was issued.

23
[116] In terms of assessing the risk of potential harm to Selectlok, the Authority was satisfied
the Mr Pearce’s employment agreement obligations and his undertaking to comply with his
contractual post-employment restraints was sufficient to protect Selectlok’s interests pending
the outcome of its substantive claims.
[117] Mr Pearce is retired and his evidence was that he was not actively involved in operating
Keyless. Mr Pearce’s evidence was that Keyless was his son Jonathan’s business, so any
restrictions on its ability to operate would affect his son and his son’s wife, Ms Thompson.
Keyless is a relatively new business, which mainly passively attracts business via its website.
There was no evidence that Keyless was selling the same products/services to the same
customers/clients as Selectlok was.
[118] The customer base for Keyless and Selectlok are also different. Keyless sells to
residential customers, property managers and sometimes locksmiths who are installing new
locks, compared to Selectlok which sells to commercial and industrial clients.
[119] Selectlok’s request for an order that Keyless cease trading until the substantive claims
have been determined is anti-competitive. Selectlok did not enter into a post-employment non-
competition or non-dealing restraint, so the relief sought would rewrite the bargain Selectlok
and Mr Pearce agreed on in their employment agreement dated 1 July 2012.
[120] The respondents provided a detailed explanation for each of Selectlok’s specific
concerns, as follows:
(a) Five of them were existing clients of Jonathan Pearce’s business LockLab,
before Keyless was incorporated.
(b) LSC and WLS remained Selectlok’s customers but they also purchased items
from Keyless that Selectlok did not offer.
(c) Two other identified clients approached Keyless through its website, so they
were not solicited.
(d) The supplier Selectlok identified as of concern had not been used by Selectlok,
so it was not a supplier or prospective supplier that was covered by the non-
solicitation restraint. That supplier also specialises in smart locks that Selectlok
does not sell.

24
(e) An advertising payment Selectlok was concerned about was for a real estate
agent in connection with a house sale, so it did not relate to Keyless.
[121] Selectlok does not sell smart locks (or associated products) to residential customers or
property managers. There was no evidence that while Mr Pearce was still employed Selectlok
had any plans to move into smart locks and/or into selling to the residential market. Nor was
there any evidence that it currently intends to do so.
[122] Keyless’ customers, clients and suppliers and would be adversely affected if the interim
injunction Selectlok sought was granted, as would Jonathan Pearce and his wife. Selectlok is
not currently able to sell the products Keyless currently supplies, so the adverse effects on these
third parties outweighs the risk of any harm Selectlok could potentially face by the interim
injunction being declined. Should Selectlok actually be harmed, then it could pursue its
damages claim.
[123] The respondents’ evidence was that Keyless is a small business that has been built on
and through Jonathan’s industry knowledge, his relationships, and his work in the smart lock
sector. Jonathan is the person who actively works in and runs the business. He is the person
principally responsible for Keyless’ supplier communications, customer communications,
product sourcing, and ordinary trading activity. His wife, Erin Thompson, also actively
contributes to the business by assisting with matters such as website content, promotional
material, and related operational support.
[124] If the Authority were to grant injunctive relief restraining Keyless from carrying on its
present activities, that would adversely affect Keyless directly and substantially. In particular,
any injunction that prevented or materially restricted Keyless from selling, promoting,
sourcing, or supplying its smart lock and digital access products would impede the continuation
of its business operations.
[125] Such an order would also likely disrupt existing and prospective dealings with Keyless’
customers, locksmith contacts, installers, and suppliers, even though those dealings concern
products that are different from Selectlok’s product lines. The practical effect of an interim
injunction could place at risk the goodwill, continuity, and commercial viability of Keyless as
a small business.

25
[126] The evidence was that provided by Mr Pearce was that an interruption to Keyless’
ability to trade would not be easily absorbed by Keyless. Restricting Keyless’ business
activities would not simply inconvenience it, but would also adversely affect the people
actively engaged in running and supporting it such as Jonathan Pearce and Erin Thompson.
[127] The likelihood of injunctive relief against Keyless causing real prejudice to third parties
outweighs the possible risk that Selectlok could suffer loss, particularly when Selectlok’s
evidence did not establish Keyless had competed with Selectlok, or had received diverted
business from Selectlok, or had received and misused Selectlok’s confidential information.
Outcome of the overall justice criteria
[128] The overall justice is strongly weighted in favour of preserving the status quo until the
substantive claims can be resolved.
Outcome
[129] The Authority does not have jurisdiction to order the respondents to provide the
undertakings Selectlok has sought in its submissions.
[130] Mr Pearce voluntarily provided an undertaking that he would comply with the post-
employment restraints in clauses 18 and 34.1 of his employment agreement, so he can be held
to that. Keyless has been transparent and co-operative by voluntarily disclosing its financial
statements and bank records.
[131] Selectlok has an arguable case that Mr Pearce breached clause 5 of his employment
agreement while he was employed. However, that potential breach was insufficient to warrant
the interim injunction Selectlok sought, as damages would likely be an adequate remedy if
Selectlok established that claim after a substantive investigation meeting has been held.
[132] Selectlok’s failure to provide the necessary evidence to establish on the balance of
probabilities that Mr Pearce had breached his post-employment restraints fundamentally
undermined its application for an interim injunction. Accordingly, the respondents have
successfully defended Selectlok’s interim injunction application, which has been declined.
